hook_text: Concrete cracks if you pull it. Steel buckles if you push it long and thin. So where does the steel go in a ramp?
clip_script: Tension is pulling: rope, cable, the steel in a beam. Steel loves it, concrete hates it. Compression is pushing: columns, walls, arches. Concrete loves it; long thin steel bows out and buckles. Now bend a plank on two bricks: top squeezed, bottom stretched, both at once. Concrete cracks on the stretched side, so that is where the mesh goes, low in the slab. A step sticking out of a wall bends the other way, so its steel goes on top. Twist is torsion: tubes resist it, which is why rails are tubes. And a rectangle of four sticks folds flat until you add one diagonal, two triangles, and it cannot move. That diagonal is the knee brace on your handrail.
visual_style: Whiteboard paper strip pulled then folded; a gridded foam beam bending with top lines closing and bottom lines opening; a rectangle racking then locking with one diagonal.
mood: Hands-on physics, satisfying clicks of understanding.
pacing: Two forces, the beam reveal, the twist, the diagonal.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and bend an eraser to find its tension face.
